title: Regression line of x on y and prediction
summary: When you know $y$ and want to estimate $x$, you need the [[regression-line-x-on-y|regression line of x on y]]. It is a different line from the one you met for predicting $y$. You learn to find it with your GDC, predict with it, and pick the right line for every prediction.

goals.text: Find the [[regression-line-x-on-y|regression line of x on y]] with your GDC, and use it to predict $x$ from a given $y$.
Choose the right regression line for a prediction, and explain why a line of $x$ on $y$ can't reliably predict $y$ from $x$.
Use the mean point, where the two regression lines cross, to find $\bar{x}$, $\bar{y}$ or a missing constant.
Judge whether a prediction is reliable: the right line, strong correlation, and a given value inside the data.

before.prompt: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = 3x - 4$, and $\bar{x} = 6$. Find $\bar{y}$.
The regression line of $y$ on $x$ makes the sum of which squared distances as small as possible?
before.hint: The line predicts $y$. Which direction is $y$ measured in on a scatter diagram?

options.text: Vertical distances from the points to the line
Horizontal distances from the points to the line
Perpendicular distances from the points to the line

before.explain: It predicts $y$, which is measured up the page, so it minimises the squared vertical distances. Revise it in {{lesson:4.4}}.

before.prompt: A line of $y$ on $x$ was built from data with $x$ between $20$ and $50$, and $r = 0.95$. How would you describe a prediction of $y$ at $x = 65$?
before.hint: Is $65$ inside or outside the range of the $x$ data?

options.text: Extrapolation, so it may be unreliable

before.explain: $65$ is outside $20$ to $50$, so it is extrapolation. A strong $r$ doesn't help outside the data. Revise it in {{lesson:4.4}}.

sections.heading: The regression line of x on y

blocks.text: A forester can measure round a tree trunk with a tape in seconds. Finding the tree's age is much harder. So she wants to predict age $x$ from circumference $y$: here $y$ is known and $x$ is the unknown.
The line of $y$ on $x$ from {{lesson:4.4}} won't do. It was built to keep the errors in $y$ small. To predict $x$, you need a line that keeps the errors in $x$ small.

blocks.term: Regression line of x on y
blocks.statement: The [[regression-line-x-on-y|regression line of x on y]] is the line $x = cy + d$ that minimises the sum of the squared horizontal distances from the points to the line. It passes through the [[mean-point|mean point]] $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
blocks.plain: The best straight line for predicting $x$ from $y$.

blocks.alt: Six points with a straight line through them. A short horizontal dashed segment joins each point to the line.
blocks.caption: The squares of these horizontal distances add up to as little as possible.

blocks.text: Here $c$ and $d$ are constants. Exam questions may use other letters, so check which variable is on the left.

blocks.question: Over $60$ days, a household recorded the mean outdoor temperature $x$ °C and its electricity use $y$ kWh. Its daily use ranged from $9$ to $27$ kWh. The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = 30 - 0.8x$, and the regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x = 31.2 - 0.9y$. Estimate the mean temperature on a day when the household used $14$ kWh.
steps: You know $y = 14$ and want $x$, so use the line of $x$ on $y$: $x = 31.2 - 0.9y$.
You were given a $y$, so check it against the range of the $y$ data. For a line of $x$ on $y$, that is the range that decides [[interpolation|interpolation]].
$14$ kWh is inside the recorded $9$ to $27$ kWh, so this is interpolation. The mean temperature was about $18.6$ °C.

check.prompt: Now you try: estimate the mean temperature, in °C, on a day when the household used $20$ kWh.
check.hint: You know $y$, so use the line of $x$ on $y$.

blocks.text: Your GDC finds the line of $x$ on $y$ with the same linear regression command as before. The only change is the lists: the $y$-values go in the X list and the $x$-values in the Y list.

blocks.question: A forester records the age $x$ years and the trunk circumference $y$ cm of eight trees. $x$: $12, 18, 25, 31, 40, 46, 55, 63$. $y$: $62, 95, 78, 124, 105, 150, 122, 168$. (a) Use your calculator to find the regression line of $x$ on $y$. (b) Estimate the age of a tree with circumference $100$ cm. Give your answers to 3 s.f.
steps: (a) You will predict $x$ from $y$, so you need the line of $x$ on $y$. Enter the circumferences ($y$) as the X list and the ages ($x$) as the Y list.
Run linear regression ($ax + b$). The screen shows $a = 0.43950\ldots$ and $b = -13.413\ldots$. These are $c$ and $d$, so the line is $x \approx 0.440y - 13.4$.
(b) Write down the substitution, using the stored values: $x = 0.43950\ldots \times 100 - 13.413\ldots$.
This gives $x = 30.536\ldots \approx 30.5$ years. $100$ cm is inside the circumferences $62$ to $168$ cm, so this is interpolation.

ti84: STAT, 1: Edit, type the circumferences into L1 and the ages into L2 (check on your model)
STAT, CALC, 4: LinReg(ax+b), Xlist: L1, Ylist: L2, move to Calculate, ENTER
Read a = 0.4395... and b = -13.41... Here a is c, the number that multiplies the circumference, and b is d
nspire: Lists & Spreadsheet page, name column A circ and column B age in the header row, then type the circumferences under circ and the ages under age (check on your model)
Menu, Statistics, Stat Calculations, Linear Regression (mx+b)
Choose circ as the X List and age as the Y List, then OK (check on your model)
Read m = 0.4395... (this is c) and b = -13.41... (this is d)
casio: STAT, type the circumferences into List 1 and the ages into List 2 (check on your model)
Read a = 0.4395... (this is c) and b = -13.41... (this is d)

blocks.text: Entering the lists in the usual order. For the line of $x$ on $y$, the $y$-values go in the X list; the usual order gives the line of $y$ on $x$.
Write the line with its constants to 3 s.f., but predict with the stored values. Rounding $c$ and $d$ first can change the last figure.

blocks.prompt: You want the regression line of $x$ on $y$ from your GDC. Which values go in the X list?
blocks.hint: The GDC always predicts its Y list from its X list. Which variable do you want to predict?

options.text: Either: both orders give the same line

blocks.explain: You want to predict $x$, so $x$ goes in the Y list and $y$ in the X list. The two orders give different lines unless $r = \pm 1$.

blocks.prompt: Use the trees' line of $x$ on $y$ to estimate the age, in years, of a tree with circumference $140$ cm. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Substitute $y = 140$ into $x = cy + d$, with the full values of $c$ and $d$.
blocks.explain: $x = 0.43950\ldots \times 140 - 13.413\ldots = 48.116\ldots \approx 48.1$ years. $140$ cm is inside the circumferences, $62$ to $168$ cm, so this is interpolation.

blocks.text: Each regression line predicts the variable named first. The line of $y$ on $x$ predicts $y$. The line of $x$ on $y$ predicts $x$.

blocks.statement: Use the line of $x$ on $y$ only to predict $x$ from a given $y$. It cannot reliably predict $y$ from a given $x$: use the line of $y$ on $x$ for that.
blocks.why: Each line keeps the errors small in the variable it predicts, and only in that variable.

blocks.text: Rearranging doesn't help. Making $y$ the subject of $x = cy + d$ gives the same line, which still minimises horizontal distances. It is not the line of $y$ on $x$.

blocks.alt: Four fixed points and one point you can drag, which starts well below the trend of the others. A solid line shows the y on x regression line and a dashed line the x on y line. Both pass through the mean point, marked with a small ring. The value of r and both equations update as you drag.

blocks.text: The ringed point starts far off the trend, so $r \approx -0.25$ and the lines cross at a wide angle. Drag it up to $(5, 6)$: $r$ rises to $0.9$ and the lines close up. The weaker the correlation, the more their predictions differ. They are one line only when $r = \pm 1$.

blocks.question: For the eight trees above, the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y \approx 1.72x + 50.7$. (a) Estimate the circumference of a $20$-year-old tree. (b) A student makes $y$ the subject of the line of $x$ on $y$ instead. Find the student's estimate, and explain why the method is not appropriate. Give your answers to 3 s.f.
steps: (a) You know $x = 20$ and want $y$, so use the line of $y$ on $x$. Run the regression with the ages in the X list, then use the stored values: $y = 1.7197\ldots \times 20 + 50.659\ldots = 85.054\ldots \approx 85.1$ cm.
(b) The student rearranges $x = 0.43950\ldots y - 13.413\ldots$ to $y = \frac{x + 13.413\ldots}{0.43950\ldots}$.
At $x = 20$: $y = \frac{33.413\ldots}{0.43950\ldots} = 76.026\ldots \approx 76.0$ cm, about $9$ cm below the estimate in (a).
The line of $x$ on $y$ keeps the errors in age small, not in circumference, so it can't reliably predict a circumference. The gap is large because $r \approx 0.869$ is well short of $1$.

blocks.question: For $35$ gardens, $x$ is the lawn area in $\text{m}^{2}$ and $y$ is the water used in litres per week. The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = 0.6x + 26$. The regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x = 1.25y - 22.5$. (a) Estimate the water used by a garden with a $30\text{ m}^{2}$ lawn. (b) Estimate the lawn area of a garden that uses $60$ litres per week.
steps: (a) You know $x$ and want $y$: use the line of $y$ on $x$. $y = 0.6 \times 30 + 26 = 18 + 26 = 44$ litres per week.
(b) You know $y$ and want $x$: use the line of $x$ on $y$. $x = 1.25 \times 60 - 22.5 = 75 - 22.5 = 52.5\text{ m}^{2}$.
Check: rearranging the line of $x$ on $y$ in (a) would give $y = \frac{30 + 22.5}{1.25} = 42$. The wrong line gives a different answer, so the choice of line matters.

blocks.prompt: For the household, $y = 30 - 0.8x$ is the line of $y$ on $x$ and $x = 31.2 - 0.9y$ is the line of $x$ on $y$. Estimate the electricity use, in kWh, on a day with mean temperature $10$ °C. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.explain: Use the line of $y$ on $x$: $y = 30 - 0.8 \times 10 = 22.0$ kWh. $23.6$ comes from rearranging the line of $x$ on $y$, and $22.2$ from putting $10$ into it as $y$.

blocks.prompt: The tree data had ages from $12$ to $63$ years and circumferences from $62$ to $168$ cm. For which estimate is the line of $x$ on $y$ the right, reliable tool?
blocks.hint: Which variable does this line predict? Is the given value inside the data?

options.text: The age of a tree with circumference $130$ cm
The age of a tree with circumference $250$ cm

blocks.explain: The line of $x$ on $y$ predicts age from circumference, and $130$ cm is inside $62$ to $168$ cm. A circumference needs the line of $y$ on $x$, and $250$ cm is extrapolation.

blocks.text: Both regression lines pass through the [[mean-point|mean point]] $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. So that is where they cross.

blocks.statement: The lines of $y$ on $x$ and of $x$ on $y$ intersect at $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. Solving their equations simultaneously gives both means.
blocks.why: Each line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, and two different straight lines meet at only one point.

blocks.question: For a set of bivariate data, the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = 0.5x + 13$. The regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x = 1.2y - 10$. Find $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$.
steps: The point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ lies on each line, so its coordinates satisfy both equations at once.
Replace $x$ in the first equation by $1.2y - 10$: $y = 0.5(1.2y - 10) + 13 = 0.6y - 5 + 13 = 0.6y + 8$.
So $0.4y = 8$, which gives $\bar{y} = 20$.
Then $\bar{x} = 1.2 \times 20 - 10 = 14$. Check in the first line: $0.5 \times 14 + 13 = 20$. Correct.

blocks.question: Five pairs of data have $y$-values $15, 17, 21, 33, 34$ and $\bar{x} = 16$. Their line of $x$ on $y$ has equation $x = 0.75y + d$. (a) Find $d$. (b) Estimate $x$ when $y = 30$.
steps: (a) The line passes through $(16, 24)$, so $16 = 0.75 \times 24 + d = 18 + d$, which gives $d = -2$.
(b) You know $y$, so this is the right line. $x = 0.75 \times 30 - 2 = 22.5 - 2 = 20.5$.
$30$ is inside the $y$-values, $15$ to $34$, so this is interpolation.

blocks.text: Substituting a data point into a regression line as if it lay on it. Only the mean point is sure to be on the line.

blocks.prompt: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = 0.4x + 9$, and the regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x = 2y - 14$. Find $\bar{x}$.
blocks.hint: Substitute one equation into the other.

blocks.prompt: The regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x = 1.5y + d$, and the mean point is $(40, 22)$. Find $d$.
blocks.hint: The mean point lies on the line, so substitute $x = 40$ and $y = 22$.

blocks.text: The line of $x$ on $y$, $x = cy + d$, minimises squared horizontal distances. Use it to predict $x$ from $y$.
On your GDC, put the $y$-values in the X list and the $x$-values in the Y list.
A line of $x$ on $y$ can't reliably predict $y$ from $x$: use the line of $y$ on $x$. Never rearrange one line to predict the other variable.
Both lines go through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$: solving the two equations together gives the means. They are one line only if $r = \pm 1$.
Trust a prediction only with strong correlation and a given value inside the range of the data. For a line of $x$ on $y$, check the $y$ data.

mistakes: Rearranging the line of $y$ on $x$ to predict $x$, or the line of $x$ on $y$ to predict $y$. Each line predicts only the variable on its left, so use the other line.
Entering the lists in the usual order. For the line of $x$ on $y$, the $y$-values go in the X list.
Mixing up the constants. Write the line out in full, such as $x = 0.440y - 13.4$, so it is clear which number multiplies $y$.
Rounding $c$ and $d$ before predicting. Use the stored values and round only the answer.
Commenting only on $r$ when asked about reliability. Also check that the given value is inside the range of the data.
examTips: Find the regression line of $x$ on $y$: write the whole equation, with $x$ on the left and constants to 3 s.f.
Give a reason a method is not appropriate: say which variable the line was built to predict, and that the question predicts the other one.
Find the means from two regression lines: both pass through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, so show the simultaneous equations you solve.
Estimate on Paper 2: write the substitution with the stored values first. The method mark depends on it.
